newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Turk Cypriot minister accused in flagpole killing.
newsitem.headline: Turk Cypriot minister accused in flagpole killing.

text.p: Greek Cypriot media alleged on Monday that a senior official in the breakaway Turkish Cypriot state in northern Cyprus was one of five people who shot dead a Greek Cypriot man as he tried to tear down a Turkish flag during protests last month.
Kenan Akin, agriculture minister in the breakaway Turkish Cypriot enclave, shot dead Greek Cypriot Solomos Solomos on August 14, state-run Cyprus Broadcasting Corporation (CyBC) reported.
It showed pictures of a man it said was Akin standing on a balcony near the flagpole and holding a pistol in front of him with both hands.
Senior Cypriot government officials, who refused to be identified, told Reuters they had information of Akin's involvement in Solomos's killing.
"We have such information in our possession," said a source. "We have photographic evidence that Akin was the person who shot Solomos."
The source said the Cyprus government had had this information for a few days and that it would be conveyed to the attorney-general.

Solomos, 26, was shot dead during demonstrations in the U.N.-patrolled buffer zone dividing Cyprus as he attempted to climb up a flagpole to remove the Turkish flag from a sentry position. CyBC said Akin was one of five people who opened fire on the youth as he was climbing up the pole.
A post-mortem on Solomos showed he had been hit by five bullets.
CyBC and government sources said Akin was a Turk who settled in Cyprus in 1974 and had served in the Turkish Secret Service, known as MIT.
Officials in the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus, which is recognised only by Turkey since its creation in 1983, were not immediately available for comment on the report.

Three days before Solomos was killed a mob of Turks battered to death Greek Cypriot Tasos Isaac with steel bars in the buffer zone near the village of Dherinia during a rally against the island's division.
Cyprus has been divided since Turkey invaded the northern third of the island in 1974 in the wake of a short-lived coup engineered by the military ruling Greece.
Tension has mounted on the island since last month's killings.
On Sunday a Turkish Cypriot soldier was found shot dead in his sentry post close to the U.N. buffer zone.
Turkish Cypriots have blamed Greek Cypriots for the killing. The Cyprus government has denied any involvement.
Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash on Monday urged Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides to hold talks with him following the latest killing.
Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller told journalists in Ankara that she would travel to Cyprus for Tuesday's funeral of Allahverdi Kilic, 20.
"We have to talk in order to cool off the heat and tension," said Denktash, head of the self-proclaimed Turkish Cypriot state.
